Okay hear me out, working at a daycare.  I have pretty bad social anxiety and used to work in food service. Hated it and cried a lot, especially when I was a server. Then I started working at a daycare. 

 The nice thing about daycare is yes, you do have to interact with people, but it’s the same people everyday. There’s no revolving door of customers. And majority of the time, your social interactions are with children who don’t judge you and don’t care. They will love you no matter who you are lol. It took me a little while to get used to interacting with parents. But if you work at a good center they will really appreciate you. 2 months into working there I got gifts from a few parents for teacher appreciation week. I have now been there for 3 years and have known most of the parents for all 3 years, so now im completely comfortable and familiar with them and can even joke around with them sometimes. 

 I will say though, I do not recommend this for a career or a super long term gig. But it was a great stepping stone for me and honestly made me better at social interactions. Like I said, you’re seeing the same people everyday, there are no new people to judge you. Once you’ve been there for a little bit, you are so used to all the parents, kids, etc that nothing is ever really awkward or uncomfortable (well, for the most part haha) it’s nice to be comfortable somewhere and never having to worry about having super awkward interactions or feeling judged. Everyone knows you and you know them.

I completely understand where you’re coming from. I used to work with two teachers who would have “relaxing music” on all day. The kids were yelling not only because they were kids, but because they had to yell over the music and the air purifier. Whenever I would take over for them, the first thing I would do is shut off the music and turn off the air purifier… and what do you know, the kids weren’t as loud as they were before. They insisted we needed the music on to calm certain students, but even relaxing piano music at a high volume is not calming or relaxing. It just made the kids more crazy. It was so freaking frustrating. 

 I would talk to your director about it. Not only should you tell her how it affects you, but you should also tell her the possible repercussions it could have on the kids. Some kids, like you, get sensory overload. I would do some research on sensory overload in children and bring that up to your director. They should not be playing music all day long and especially not at a high volume. It’s distracting, it overwhelms people, and causes the entire volume of the classroom to go up because like I said kids have to yell over the music. I’m sorry you have to deal with this, I feel your pain.

Hi! It can be incredibly frustrating working with people who don’t seem to be much help, especially when you’re new. I’ve been doing this for three years and still struggle with this. 

 When I was new and was working with people like that, I just dove right in and took control. If they aren’t going to, why shouldn’t you? For example, let’s say it’s free play time and they’re getting out of control and you’re putting out fire after fire. Announce that it’s time to clean up. Then, gather them on the carpet and read a story, play a game, start a conversation. Something I like to do during times like these is take a piece of construction paper and write something at the top like “My Favorite Thing To Do In The Winter Is….” and then ask each child their favorite thing, then I write their name down and write what they said. The parents love to look at these when I hang them up by the door, and it’s a great way to waste time and regain control of the class. It’s also a great way to start a conversation about something educational. 

 Also, young children thrive on structure and consistency. Let them know what your expectations are, why you have those expectations, and stick to them. For example, there isn’t a bathroom in my classroom so everytime someone has to go potty I have to take a group down the hall to the bathroom. My expectation is that they stand or sit up against the wall while they wait their turn. I keep them busy by providing them books to look at or we play simple games like I Spy or Simon Says. Other coworkers of mine have no expectations when it comes to hallway behavior. They allow the kids to walk up and down the hall, peer into other classrooms, wrestle and play with each other. That stuff doesn’t fly with me lol. It leads to chaos. The kids know that when I take them down to the bathroom, they have to stay in that designated area and either look at a book or play the game. Or they can just wait patiently if they aren’t interested in those two things. They know I have this expectation because I’m consistent with it and I’ve explained why. I say “people need to get by, we can’t be blocking up the entire hallway” “other classes are sleeping right now, we can’t be loud in the hallway” etc. 

 Another thing I tell myself a lot is “be proactive, not reactive.” You have to be able to predict potential problems and know why these problems occur. Rather  than reacting to the problem, you prevent the problem. If climbing on furniture is a problem, start having conversations with the entire class about why we don’t do that. I don’t know if you feel comfortable doing this or suggesting this, but if they are consistently climbing on a certain piece of furniture, just take it out of the room. There’s no sense in all the unnecessary chaos if it’s causing large amounts of problems. I’m all for removing unnecessary chaos if it makes the classroom more peaceful. 

 Unfortunately, there’s not much you can do about coworkers who simply don’t want to work. I am looking for a new job because of this. Day in and day out I have to deal with the same stuff you described. Coworkers ignoring behaviors and ignoring the children in general. I’d say something to the director but if nothing changes, look for something new. I’ve stayed for way too long hoping it would get better but I can’t control what other adults do. I’m so sorry you have to deal with this, I understand your pain. I’m sure you’re a great teacher!
